title: The GenAI Maturity Curve or  You Probably Don't Need Fine Tuning: Kyle Corbitt
talk_summary: A fine-tuning vendor argues most teams should start with prompted frontier models and only fine-tune once product shape is stable, driven by cost, latency, or consistency needs. The transferable mechanism is using expensive multi-pass LLM generation to produce high-quality training/eval data, then distilling into a cheaper model.

takeaways.technique: Distill expensive multi-pass outputs into a cheap model
takeaways.what_they_do: Use a costly multi-iteration 'mixture of agents' prompting pipeline to generate high-quality labeled outputs, then fine-tune a small cheap model on that data to move the cost/quality Pareto frontier outward.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you then take say you found way like using this mixture of experts to get or sorry mixture of agents to get really high quality data
takeaways.numbers: claims '125th the cost' better performance than GPT-4 (vendor claim, unverified)

takeaways.what_they_do: Split evals into fast LLM-judge inner-loop checks run on every change, and business-specific outer-loop evals that require deployment/AB testing.
takeaways.evidence_quote: inner loop evaluations just mean something you can run really fast and get feedback on fast

takeaways.technique: Log all prompts as training/eval corpus
takeaways.what_they_do: Log every production prompt and response to a database/observability store so you can later characterize the real input distribution and build datasets.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you just every time you do a prompt you throw it in there

takeaways.what_they_do: Start with a general prompted model for iteration speed, and only specialize/optimize once the task shape is stable and volume justifies it.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you can get away with a prompted model to start with um you should do that
